title: Quedar vs Quedarse: Meet, Stay, Fit and More
seo_title: Quedar vs Quedarse: Meet, Stay, Fit and More
meta_description: Quedar vs quedarse: quedarse means to stay or keep, while quedar means to meet up, be left, suit or be located. Clear examples, regional notes and a quiz.
excerpt: One little “se” changes everything. A clear guide to two of the most useful Spanish verbs.

body_html:
Quedar vs quedarse is a pair where a tiny se changes the meaning completely. Quedarse mostly means to stay or to keep something, while quedar means to arrange to meet, to be left over, to suit someone or to be located somewhere. Both are everywhere in everyday Spanish, so learning their main uses will instantly make your Spanish more natural.

Quick answer
  • Quedarse = to stay, remain: Me quedo en casa.
  • Quedarse con = to keep: Me quedo con este.
  • Quedar = to meet up (Spain), to be left, to suit, to be located.
  • Quedarse + adjective = to end up: quedarse dormido (to fall asleep).
{{toc}}

Quedar vs quedarse at a glance

MeaningVerbExample
To stay, remainquedarseNos quedamos tres días en Lima. We stayed three days in Lima.
To keepquedarse conQuédate con el cambio. Keep the change.
To end up (state)quedarseMe quedé dormido. I fell asleep.
To arrange to meetquedar¿Quedamos a las siete? Shall we meet at seven?
To be leftquedarQuedan dos entradas. There are two tickets left.
To suit, fitquedarTe queda genial. It looks great on you.
To be locatedquedar¿Dónde queda el museo? Where is the museum?
To agree onquedar enQuedamos en vernos el lunes. We agreed to meet on Monday.

The RAE dictionary lists more than twenty senses for quedar, which shows how much work this verb does in Spanish.

Quedarse: staying and keeping

  • Hoy me quedo en casa. I’m staying home today.
  • ¿Te quedas a cenar? Are you staying for dinner?
  • Me quedo con la camisa azul. I’ll take (keep) the blue shirt.
  • Quédate tranquilo. Don’t worry (stay calm).

Quedarse + adjective: ending up in a state

  • quedarse dormido to fall asleep / oversleep
  • quedarse sin batería to run out of battery
  • quedarse sin palabras to be left speechless
  • quedarse embarazada to get pregnant
  • quedarse callado to go quiet
{{image:2}}

Quedar: meeting, leftovers, fit and location

To meet up (especially in Spain)

In Spain, quedar is the everyday verb for making plans: ¿Quedamos mañana? (Shall we meet tomorrow?), He quedado con Ana para comer (I’ve arranged to have lunch with Ana). In much of Latin America people more often say ¿Nos vemos mañana? or ¿Quedamos? is understood but less frequent.

To be left

¿Queda leche? (Is there any milk left?) / Me quedan diez euros. (I have ten euros left.) This works like gustar: what remains is the subject.

To suit or fit

Ese color te queda muy bien. (That colour really suits you.) / Los pantalones me quedan grandes. (The trousers are too big for me.)

To be located (Latin America especially)

¿Dónde queda el banco? (Where is the bank?) / Queda a dos cuadras. (It’s two blocks away.)

{{book:love-slowly}}

Real conversations

Making plans in Spain

  • A: ¿Quedamos el sábado para tomar algo? (Shall we meet on Saturday for a drink?)
  • B: Vale, pero no puedo quedarme hasta tarde. (Okay, but I can’t stay late.)
  • A: Sin problema. ¿Quedamos en la plaza a las ocho? (No problem. Shall we meet in the square at eight?)

Shopping

  • Friend: Ese vestido te queda perfecto. (That dress fits you perfectly.)
  • You: ¿Sí? Pues me lo quedo. (Really? Then I’ll take it.)

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Quedo en casa hoy.Me quedo en casa hoy.Staying needs quedarse
Me quedo con Ana a las seis. (meaning meet)Quedo con Ana a las seis.Quedarse con means to keep
El vestido queda bien para mí.El vestido me queda bien.Use an indirect object pronoun
Dormí y me quedé tarde.Me quedé dormido.Oversleeping is quedarse dormido

That second mistake can be funny: Me quedo con Ana sounds like “I’m keeping Ana”.

{{image:3}}

A quick mental shortcut

Ask whether the subject is a person choosing to remain or keep something. If so, it is almost always quedarse: me quedo, te quedas, se queda con el libro. If the subject is a thing that is left over, a piece of clothing that fits, a place that is located somewhere or a plan between friends, use quedar. A simple test sentence: Quedé con Lucía, pero al final me quedé en casa (I arranged to meet Lucía, but in the end I stayed home).

Try it yourself

  1. Are you staying for coffee? (¿Te quedas a tomar un café?)
  2. There are only five minutes left. (Solo quedan cinco minutos.)
  3. Those shoes look great on you. (Esos zapatos te quedan genial.)
  4. We agreed to call each other. (Quedamos en llamarnos.)
  5. My phone ran out of battery. (Me quedé sin batería.)

Quedar vs quedarse is part of a bigger family of verbs whose meaning changes with se; compare {{link:salir-vs-irse|salir vs irse}} and {{link:ponerse-volverse-hacerse|ponerse, volverse and hacerse}}, or see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Remember the anchor: quedarse is staying and keeping; quedar is meeting, being left, fitting and being located. With those five meanings you can make plans, shop and give directions like a native speaker.

faq.q: What is the difference between quedar and quedarse?
faq.a: Quedarse means to stay or remain, and quedarse con means to keep. Quedar means to arrange to meet, to be left over, to suit or fit, or to be located.

faq.q: How do you say “let’s meet” in Spanish?
faq.a: In Spain, ¿Quedamos? is the most common. In much of Latin America, ¿Nos vemos? is more usual.
It means to fall asleep, and often to oversleep: Me quedé dormido y llegué tarde.

questions.q: In Spain: ¿___ mañana para comer? (Shall we meet tomorrow?)

questions.explain: The jacket is the subject: it suits you. Te queda.

questions.explain: What remains is the subject: te queda.
